newsitem.title: FINLAND: U.S. offers Russia arms START-2 arms concession.
newsitem.headline: U.S. offers Russia arms START-2 arms concession.

text.p: In a bid to persuade Russia to ratify a nuclear arms treaty, the United States has offered to let Moscow delay a deadline that might require the U.S. Senate to vote on the deal again, U.S. officials said on Thursday.

The officials said the proposal was advanced during last weekend's talks in Washington between Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and is to be discussed at Friday's summit talks between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

It is among the concessions offered by Washington in an effort to win an "unequivocal commitment" from Yeltsin that the Russian parliament (Duma) vote soon on the long-delayed treaty -- the START-2 strategic arms reduction treaty.

The agreement was signed in 1993 and builds on an initial agreement to cut missiles. START-2 would cut warheads for long-range missiles on each side to no more than 3,500 by the year 2003, a third of the Cold War level.

Washington has already said it is ready to negotiate even deeper cuts if START-2 is ratified by the hostile Duma, where communists and nationalists say the treaty puts Russia at a severe disadvantage.

The U.S. proposals could make START-2 more palatable to Russia but could also upset American critics who fear Clinton is bending too far in trying to get Moscow to accept plans for NATO's eastward expansion.
A new START-3 treaty, according to the U.S. proposal, would aim to reduce U.S. and Russian arsenals to between 2,000 and 2,500 warheads per side.

Although reaching some accommodation on NATO expansion plans is the centrepiece of the summit, arms control is also an important subtext because it affects Russia's perception of its security and its willingness to deal on NATO expansion.
The latest compromise involves a U.S. offer to let Moscow delay by a few years, beyond the current deadline of 2003, the destruction of missile silos under the START-2 treaty.
Russia must still dismantle thousands of nuclear warheads by 2003 because those go to the heart of the nuclear danger, officials said.

Although it might be possible to handle the deadline change on silos through a new treaty cutting nuclear arms, senior officials said on Thursday they were now looking at possibly amending START-2 -- already approved by the U.S. Senate.
This could be risky because the Senate is controlled by Republicans who have opposed Clinton on many issues and refused to ratify another arms agreement on chemical weapons.
Putting an amended START-2 before the Senate could therefore be a real gamble.
Underlining this, Republican leaders in Washington warned Clinton on Thursday not to make too many concessions to Yeltsin on the related issue of missile defence systems.

But officials said there may be other ways to handle the proposed change. It could be judged by arms control lawyers to be a technical change not requiring further action or it could be approved by a commission set up to adjudicate treaty disagreements, one official said.

"The Senate is not likely to be disposed to give more time on the destruction deadlines unless you can demonstrate that the warheads, which are after all the source of the nuclear danger here, are going to come off on time," another official said.
"So we think that's the tradeoff that would enable us to go back to the Senate and get their approval to extend the deadline on the silos destruction," he said.
